lead: React and Angular are the two front-end frameworks that Indian full-stack job ads ask for most. This unit builds the same ideas twice, first in React and then in Angular with TypeScript: components, data flow, routing, forms, shared state and API calls. After it you can write a small single-page app, route it, manage its state, make it work offline and wire it to a REST API.
about: The unit moves from one React component to a complete front-end application. 5.1 builds components with JSX, 5.2 gives them props and state, and 5.3 wires them to clicks and forms. 5.4 puts many components behind a router, so a URL decides what renders. 5.5 steps aside to TypeScript, the typed JavaScript that Angular is written in, and 5.6 uses it to build Angular components, templates, directives and bindings. 5.7 makes the app installable and offline-first with a service worker, and fast on first paint with server-side rendering. 5.8 collects shared state into a Redux store. 5.9 closes with Angular services, dependency injection, RxJS and the HTTP client talking to a REST API.

chapters.idea: A React app is a tree of small functions called components, and each one returns JSX that React turns into real DOM elements.
chapters.depth: What React is and the problem it solves: hand-written DOM updates (Unit 3) become hard to reason about once a page has many parts, because you must remember to update every affected node yourself. React re-renders a component when its data changes, and you only describe what the screen should look like. Setup with a CDN script tag, and with Vite or create-react-app; the entry point ReactDOM.createRoot(document.getElementById('root')).render(<App />). JSX rules: one parent element or an empty fragment <></>, curly braces for JavaScript expressions, className instead of class, htmlFor instead of for, every tag closed, first letter capital means a component and lowercase means an HTML tag; Babel or the bundler converts JSX to React.createElement(type, props, ...children). Components: function components as the default, class components with a render() method (some syllabi call these React Classes), composing components by nesting them inside each other. The ES6 pieces React leans on: arrow functions, let and const, destructuring, spread, modules — one revision line each, full treatment in Unit 3. Styling in React: an external CSS file used through className, an inline style object with camelCase keys such as style={{color: 'teal'}}, CSS modules, and one line each on styled-components and Reactstrap for Bootstrap. Depth: read and write a five-component page, with no state and no hooks yet.
chapters.figure: tree (box): AppComponent at the root, with Header, PostList and Footer as children; PostList has three children, Post 1, Post 2 and Post 3. It shows that a page is a tree of components, not one long file.
chapters.example: Convert this JSX into React.createElement calls, then into the HTML the browser finally shows. JSX: <div className="card"><h2>{title}</h2><p>2 items</p></div> with title = "Dosa". Step 1: React.createElement("div", {className: "card"}, React.createElement("h2", null, "Dosa"), React.createElement("p", null, "2 items")). Step 2: the browser receives <div class="card"><h2>Dosa</h2><p>2 items</p></div>. Note that className in JSX became class in the DOM, and that the value of title was filled in from JavaScript.
chapters.trap: JSX looks like HTML but is not HTML: class must be written className, two sibling elements need one parent or a fragment, and <Greeting /> renders your component while <greeting /> is treated as an unknown HTML tag because of the lowercase first letter.
chapters.prereq: Unit 2 (HTML elements and attributes) and Unit 3 (ES6 functions, arrow functions and modules).
chapters.leave: DOM methods such as querySelector and innerHTML belong to Unit 3; CSS layout, Flexbox and Bootstrap to Unit 2.

chapters.idea: Props are read-only data passed down from a parent, state is data a component owns and changes, and changing state makes React render that component again.
chapters.depth: Props: passing values and functions, destructuring in the parameter list, the special children prop, default values, the read-only rule, PropTypes in one line. State: useState with array destructuring, const [count, setCount] = useState(0); the initial value is used only on the first render, which is what syllabi call async state initialisation; setState is asynchronous and batched, so use the updater form setCount(c => c + 1) whenever the new value depends on the old one; never mutate an object or array in state, copy it with spread. Lifting state up to the closest common parent. Stateless (presentational) versus stateful (container) components, and dynamic composition with children plus conditional rendering. Lists and keys. Class lifecycle: constructor, render, componentDidMount, componentDidUpdate(prevProps, prevState), componentWillUnmount; useEffect(fn, deps) as the hook version, where an empty array means run once and a returned cleanup function means run on unmount. Depth: write one component with two useState values and one useEffect that fetches on mount and cleans up.
chapters.figure: blocks (down): Mount → render() → componentDidMount → state/props change → render() again → componentDidUpdate, with a dashed back edge from componentDidUpdate to state/props change, and a final branch Unmount → componentWillUnmount.
chapters.example: A counter starts at count = 0. One click handler runs setCount(count + 1) three times. All three calls read count = 0 from the current render, React batches them, and after the click count is 1, not 3. Change the three calls to setCount(c => c + 1) and React queues them as 0 → 1 → 2 → 3, so count is 3.
chapters.trap: Mutating state keeps the same reference, so React sees no change and does not re-render: arr.push(item) or this.state.count = 5 fails silently. Also, reading count on the line after setCount still gives the old value, because the update is queued, not applied.
chapters.prereq: 5.1 for components and JSX, and Unit 3 for arrow functions and array destructuring.
chapters.leave: App-wide shared state is 5.8; fetching data from a server is 5.9 and Unit 6.

chapters.idea: React attaches camelCase event props to JSX, and a form input is controlled by state so that state, not the browser, holds the current value.
chapters.depth: Events: onClick={handleClick} passes a function, onClick={handleClick()} calls it during render; the synthetic event object, e.preventDefault(), e.target.value and e.target.name; passing an argument with an arrow wrapper, onClick={() => remove(id)}. Child-to-parent communication, which syllabi word as communicating from child to parent: the parent passes a callback prop, the child calls it with a value. Forms: controlled components with value plus onChange, one handler using [e.target.name]: e.target.value for many fields, textarea, select, checkbox with checked, radio groups; uncontrolled components with useRef; onSubmit with preventDefault; simple validation messages. File inputs are always uncontrolled, in one line. Depth: build a two-field login form with validation and a child that reports its value upward.
chapters.figure: sequence: actors User, Input and React state. Messages: User types R; Input fires onChange; the handler calls setName('R'); React re-renders the input with value='R'; the input shows R.
chapters.example: A login form starts with state {email: '', password: ''}. The user types ravi@example.com: onChange fires once per keystroke, e.target.name is 'email', so after the last keystroke state is {email: 'ravi@example.com', password: ''}. On submit, a password of pass123 (7 characters) passes a length ≥ 6 check, while 123 shows 'Password too short' and preventDefault stops the page reload.
chapters.trap: onClick={handleClick()} runs the handler on every render instead of on click, and an input that has value but no onChange is read-only — the user types and nothing appears, with a React warning in the console.
chapters.prereq: 5.2 for state and the updater form.
chapters.leave: GET and POST form processing on the server belongs to Unit 4; server-side validation and sessions to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: A client-side router reads the URL and decides which component to show, without asking the server for a new HTML page.
chapters.depth: Why: a single-page app loads one HTML file and swaps views, so a full page reload loses state and feels slow. React Router: install react-router-dom, wrap the app in BrowserRouter, declare Routes and Route with path and element (older versions used Switch and component or render props; name both, since syllabi differ); index routes, nested routes with Outlet, layout routes, dynamic segments /posts/:id read with useParams, Link and NavLink instead of an anchor, useNavigate for programmatic navigation after a submit, Navigate for redirects, path="*" for a 404 page, React.lazy for lazy loading in one line. Angular Router: RouterModule.forRoot(routes) or provideRouter, the routes array of {path, component} or loadComponent, router-outlet, routerLink and routerLinkActive, wildcard '**', redirectTo, ActivatedRoute params, guards in one line. Hash routing versus history routing, and the server rule that every path must return index.html. Depth: a five-route app with one parameterised route and one 404 route, in both frameworks.
chapters.figure: tree (box): a router root with four route children — / → Home, /posts → PostList, /posts/:id → PostDetail, * → NotFound. It shows that the URL picks one branch of the component tree.
chapters.example: Route table: / → Home, /posts → PostList, /posts/:id → PostDetail, * → NotFound. The user clicks a Link to /posts/42. The router matches /posts/:id, useParams() returns {id: '42'}, and PostDetail fetches post 42. Typing /blog matches * and shows NotFound, while the server still answers 200 with index.html.
chapters.trap: Using <a href="/posts"> instead of <Link to="/posts"> makes the browser fetch the page again, so the app restarts with empty state; and on a hard refresh of /posts/42 the web server must return index.html, otherwise it answers 404 because no such file exists on disk.
chapters.prereq: 5.1 for components, and Unit 1 for URLs and HTTP requests.
chapters.leave: Server-side routes in Express are Unit 6; status codes are Unit 1; server-side rendering is 5.7.

chapters.idea: TypeScript is JavaScript plus type annotations that a compiler checks before the code runs, then strips away completely.
chapters.depth: Why it exists: wrong arguments and misspelled properties are caught at compile time, and the editor can autocomplete fields. Compiling: tsc and tsconfig.json with target and strict, .ts files becoming .js files, all types erased at run time. Annotations: let n: number, string, boolean, number[] and Array<number>, tuples [string, number], any, unknown, never, void, unions 'small' | 'large', literal types, optional ? and readonly, null and undefined under strictNullChecks. Functions: parameter types, return types, optional and default parameters, function type syntax. Interfaces and type aliases, extending, structural typing, index signatures in one line. Enums, numeric and string. Classes: public, private, protected, readonly, implements, and generics with identity<T>(x: T): T and a simple Box<T>. Type inference and when to annotate anyway. Depth: enough to read Angular code comfortably and to type a small module; no decorators here and no advanced conditional or mapped types.
chapters.figure: blocks (down): app.ts → tsc type check, branching to Errors (compile stops) and to app.js with the types removed → Browser runs it. It shows that every type disappears before the browser sees the file.
chapters.example: function add(a: number, b: number): number { return a + b; } — add(2, 3) compiles and returns 5. add('2', 3) fails at compile time because a string is not assignable to a number, even though plain JavaScript would silently return '23'. Interface User { id: number; name: string; email?: string } accepts { id: 7, name: 'Ravi' } and rejects { id: '7', name: 'Ravi' } because the id is a string.
chapters.trap: An interface or type alias does not exist after compilation, so it cannot be used in a run-time check; and any switches checking off for everything it touches, hiding the bug exactly where you stopped typing.
chapters.prereq: Unit 3 for variables, functions, ES6 classes and modules.
chapters.leave: Angular's use of these types is 5.6 and 5.9; project scaffolding with the Angular CLI is 5.6.

chapters.idea: An Angular component is a TypeScript class plus an HTML template joined by a decorator, and a few kinds of binding keep the class and the template in step.
chapters.depth: The @Component decorator with selector, templateUrl and styleUrls; the CLI project layout (src/app, main.ts, angular.json); NgModule declarations versus standalone components, both named because syllabi differ. Angular versus AngularJS, said plainly: AngularJS is 1.x, in JavaScript, with ng-app, controllers and $scope; Angular is 2 and later, a rewrite in TypeScript built on components. Template syntax: interpolation {{ value }}, property binding [src]="url" and [disabled]="flag", attribute, class and style binding, event binding (click)="save()" with $event, two-way binding [(ngModel)] which needs FormsModule. Directives: structural *ngIf with an else template, *ngFor with index and trackBy, *ngSwitch; attribute directives ngClass, ngStyle, ngModel; a custom directive with @Directive and @HostListener in one line. Pipes: date, uppercase, and currency with the rupee symbol, {{ price | currency:'INR' }}. Communication: @Input() data in, @Output() with EventEmitter out. Lifecycle hooks ngOnInit, ngOnChanges and ngOnDestroy, cross-referenced to 5.2. One line each on Angular Material and Flex-Layout.
chapters.figure: blocks (right): Component class → Template → DOM, with a back edge from Template to Component class. The forward edge is interpolation and [property] binding; the back edge is (event) binding and [(ngModel)].
chapters.example: A ProductCard component has @Input() product = {id: 3, name: 'Filter coffee', price: 2499}. Its template shows <span>{{ product.price | currency:'INR' }}</span>, which renders ₹2,499.00, and a button with (click)="add.emit(product)" that sends {id: 3, name: 'Filter coffee', price: 2499} to the parent's handler when clicked.
chapters.trap: Writing AngularJS answers (ng-app, $scope, ng-controller) in an Angular 2+ question scores nothing, because they are different frameworks. Also, [(ngModel)] silently does nothing if FormsModule is not imported, and *ngFor over objects without trackBy rebuilds every row on each change.
chapters.prereq: 5.5 for TypeScript classes, interfaces and decorators; Unit 2 for HTML and CSS in templates.
chapters.leave: Services, dependency injection and HTTP are 5.9; the Angular router is 5.4; RxJS operators are 5.9.

chapters.idea: A progressive web app adds a manifest and a service worker so it installs and works offline, while server-side rendering sends finished HTML so the first screen appears before any JavaScript runs.
chapters.depth: PWA criteria: served over HTTPS, a web app manifest (name, icons, start_url, display), and a service worker; the install prompt and add-to-home-screen. Service worker: a script in its own thread with no DOM access, lifecycle install → activate → fetch, the Cache API, cache.addAll for the app shell, cache-first versus network-first versus stale-while-revalidate, an offline fallback page, versioned cache names and deleting old caches on activate; a Lighthouse audit in one line. Why Next.js appears in PWA syllabi: it gives routing plus server rendering out of the box. SSR: the single-page app problem that index.html is nearly empty, so first paint waits for JavaScript and crawlers see nothing; ReactDOMServer.renderToString and hydrateRoot on the client; a comparison table of CSR, SSR and SSG on first paint, SEO and server load; hydration mismatch warnings; getServerSideProps and getStaticProps in one line; Angular Universal in one line.
chapters.figure: sequence: actors Page, Service worker, Cache, Server. A fetch for /index.html is a cache hit served offline; a fetch for /api/price is a cache miss that goes to the server and is stored.
chapters.example: First visit online: the app shell is index.html 4 KB, app.js 120 KB and style.css 8 KB, so cache.addAll stores 132 KB. Later, in airplane mode, the reload is served from the cache and the app opens. The /api/price call misses the cache, the network fails, and the offline fallback shows the last stored price.
chapters.trap: A service worker cannot control the very first page load: it needs one visit to install, and a reload before it takes over. And caching index.html forever serves an old app after a deploy unless the cache name is versioned.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 for HTTP requests, responses and HTTPS; 5.4 for single-page apps.
chapters.leave: CI/CD and cloud deployment are Unit 6; HTTP cache headers are Unit 1.

chapters.idea: Redux keeps all shared state in one store that only a pure reducer can replace, so every change goes through a plain, traceable action.
chapters.depth: The problem it solves: prop drilling through many levels, two siblings needing the same data, and bugs that are hard to reproduce. Flux architecture: actions → dispatcher → stores → views, with one-directional flow; Redux simplified it to one store and reducers instead of a dispatcher. Redux pieces: the store, an action {type, payload}, action creators, a reducer(state = initialState, action) that is pure and returns a new object, a switch on action.type whose default returns state unchanged, combineReducers, dispatch, getState, subscribe. React-Redux: Provider around the app with useSelector and useDispatch (older connect and mapStateToProps named too). Immutability with spread for objects and arrays, never push. Async with redux-thunk in one line, Redux Toolkit createSlice in one line, middleware and DevTools in one line. The Context API as the built-in lighter option, and when Redux is overkill. Depth: write a cart reducer with two action types and trace three dispatches; no middleware code.
chapters.figure: blocks (down): View (React) → dispatch(action) → Reducer (pure) → New store state, with a back edge from the store to the view labelled subscribe → re-render. It shows the one-way loop that replaces scattered setState calls.
chapters.example: Cart state {items: [], count: 0, total: 0}. dispatch({type: 'ADD_ITEM', payload: {id: 1, name: 'Masala dosa', price: 60}}) makes the reducer return {items: [{id: 1, name: 'Masala dosa', price: 60}], count: 1, total: 60}. A second dispatch with {id: 2, name: 'Filter coffee', price: 40} returns count: 2 and total: 100. The old state object is never edited; a new object is returned each time.
chapters.trap: A reducer that pushes into the existing array or edits state.count returns the same reference, so React-Redux sees no change and the screen stays stale; and an action must be a plain object with a type, because Redux throws when type is undefined.
chapters.prereq: 5.2 for props, state and lifting state up; 5.3 for event handlers that dispatch.
chapters.leave: Server state, caching and REST calls are 5.9 and Unit 6; the URL as state stays with the router in 5.4.

chapters.idea: An Angular service is a class marked @Injectable that the injector creates once and hands to any component that asks, and RxJS Observables carry the asynchronous results of its HTTP calls.
chapters.depth: Services: why they exist, to share logic and data between components and keep components thin; @Injectable({providedIn: 'root'}) giving one instance for the whole app; constructor injection with private productService: ProductService; the providers array and hierarchical injectors in one line; easier unit testing in one line. HttpClient: provideHttpClient() or HttpClientModule, get<T>(url), post, put, delete, each returning Observable<T>; subscribe(next, error); the async pipe and its automatic unsubscribe. RxJS: Observable versus Promise (lazy, many values, cancellable), operators inside .pipe() — map, filter, tap, catchError returning of([]), retry(2), switchMap for a search, debounceTime(300), Subject versus BehaviorSubject for shared state, takeUntil with ngOnDestroy to unsubscribe. Interceptors in one line. Error handling for 404 and 500 in the error callback. Depth: one service with a GET and a POST, a component that subscribes, and a debounced search; no marble diagrams.
chapters.figure: sequence: actors Component, ProductService, HttpClient, REST API. The component calls getProducts(), the service calls HttpClient.get&t;Product[]>(url), the API answers 200 with 3 items, and the Observable emits back into subscribe.
chapters.example: A search box calls search(term) on every keystroke. Typing dosa sends 4 letters, so without debounceTime there are 4 GETs: /api/search?q=d, q=do, q=dos, q=dosa. With .pipe(debounceTime(300), switchMap(...)) and each letter arriving within 300 ms of the last, only 1 GET fires, for q=dosa, and earlier in-flight requests are cancelled. A GET that returns 500 goes to catchError, which returns of([]) so the list shows empty instead of crashing.
chapters.trap: An Observable does nothing until it is subscribed, so calling getProducts() and stopping there returns no data; and a subscription started in ngOnInit keeps running after the component is destroyed unless you unsubscribe or use the async pipe, which leaks memory.
chapters.prereq: 5.6 for Angular components and @Input, 5.5 for TypeScript generics, and Unit 6 for REST endpoints and JSON.
chapters.leave: Building the Express routes and the database behind them is Unit 6; JWT tokens and auth headers are Unit 6.

links: components become useful once they receive props and hold state
state changes happen inside event handlers, and forms are state plus onChange
a submitted form navigates to another route with useNavigate
the single-page app that the router switches is exactly what a service worker caches
Angular components are TypeScript classes with typed @Input fields
components stay thin by calling an injected service instead of fetching themselves
form state shared across many components grows into a Redux store
